A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Persona2Web. All 24 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent evaluations, human-alignment meta-evaluation, ambiguity and context experiments, retriever ablation, and error analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds dataset validation, human realism judgments, repeated executions, temporal comparisons, and judge-reliability results.

M1.justification: The history-generation pipeline, planner–retriever–generator architecture, retrieval mechanism, and history-access schemes are retained. Appendix A.2 newly documents construction checks without establishing that the underlying method was revised.

E1.justification: The 50-user benchmark, 105 websites, 21 domains, and ambiguity tasks remain unchanged. Section 5.6 adds evaluation across December 2025 and March 2026 open-web conditions, extending temporal scenario coverage. New dataset statistics do not establish additional domains or users.

E2.justification: The main agent and meta-evaluation comparator sets are retained. Appendix A.2 adds histories generated without the multi-stage pipeline as a realism comparator. Appendix B.3 newly compares GPT-5-mini with Qwen-80B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-120B as alternative judges.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include sequence- and entry-level realism comparisons by six human judges, semantic and lexical diversity measurements, evaluation across two time periods, and comparisons of alternative judges on fixed trajectories. These substantially extend validation protocols while retaining the original benchmark settings and scoring rubrics.

E4.justification: Section 5.6 and Appendices A.2–B add substantial analyses of execution and temporal robustness, history diversity and realism, human-reference agreement, and judge consistency. The earlier ambiguity, explicit-profile, retriever-indexing, and error analyses remain present.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports three-run execution and judge-evaluation means with standard deviations, human agreement using Gwet’s AC1, and inter-judge agreement using Krippendorff’s alpha and ICC (Tables 8 and 11–14). These expand v1’s point-estimate reporting; they do not establish increased run counts for the retained original results.

E6.justification: Original main, meta-evaluation, explicit-profile, and retriever-ablation scores are unchanged. Substantial new results include a 3.56% preference exact-match ratio, realism win rates of 88.3% and 98.3%, and reliability estimates. Table 9 newly reports GPT-4.1 success differences of -0.108 and -0.112 across periods, rather than revising the original benchmark scores.

T1.justification: The profile/event-generation equations and personalization, intent, and success definitions are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears; the added diversity and agreement statistics serve empirical validation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same benchmark novelty, clarify-to-personalize principle, and reasoning-aware evaluation claims. Added validation supports these contributions without redefining their core scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations that diversity and realism validate the synthetic histories, repeated and temporal evaluations establish stability, and inter-judge agreement demonstrates robustness. It qualifies intent agreement as tentative. The temporal-stability interpretation does not adequately address the sizable success-rate changes in Table 9.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 newly specifies GPT-5 construction checks and five human profile-validation criteria with revision and rechecking. The embedded CODE link changes from an anonymous repository to a named project website. Existing implementation settings and prompts remain unchanged; destination availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds supporting literature on history diversity, judge reliability, dynamic environments, and personalization errors, including PersonaLens, AndroidWorld, and AgenticShop. The central related-work positioning remains unchanged. Numerous other reference changes update publication metadata for already cited works.

P1.justification: The existing narrative is largely retained with localized edits. v2 adds Section 5.6, dataset-validation and judge-validation subsections, reorganizes appendix headings, and updates acknowledgements and conference front matter. The added scientific material does not entail extensive rewriting of the original paper.

P2.justification: New table groups present dataset composition, repeated and temporal results, and dataset/judge validation, substantially expanding the evidence displayed (Tables 3–4 and 8–14). Existing material is reflowed and renumbered. Figure 2 revises its navigation example; the other figures and original case-study displays are retained.

improvement.justification: The added human-realism, agreement, and repeated-evaluation evidence strengthens support for the dataset and scoring framework. However, Section 5.6 overstates temporal stability despite Table 9’s 10.8–11.2 percentage-point GPT-4.1 success drops. Appendix B.3 also overstates preference-score reliability: both alpha values fall below its stated 0.800 threshold. These interpretive weaknesses limit the overall gain.
